conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to check on how you’re feeling emotionally. Over the next few minutes I’ll ask you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a quick, ten-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and thoughts you may have had in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays strictly between us unless you give permission otherwise. I’ll read each question conversationally; just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very much at all. I used to laugh pretty easily—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but lately it feels like nothing’s funny anymore. I might smile once or twice if something’s really silly, but most of the time I’m just too tired or down to laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t. Maybe once or twice something small made me crack a smile, but it’s like the joy is stuck—nothing really feels funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. Before the baby I’d get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet evening. This week, when I think about doing anything, it feels flat, like “what’s the point?” I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Even when my partner says he’s just being a normal newborn, I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind just keeps spinning—Is he breathing okay? Am I holding him too much or too little? What if I miss some sign that he’s sick? There’s no real reason, but the thoughts keep looping and I can’t shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. Sometimes—especially at night when I’m trying to settle the baby—my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the fear just hits me out of nowhere, and for a minute I feel like something awful is about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep, and the constant worry, it feels like I’m drowning a little. Some moments I can talk myself down, but overall it’s a lot—like I’m always one step behind and can’t quite catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying about what might go wrong tomorrow. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and if I wake up to use the bathroom or hear him stir, those same thoughts snap right back and I’m wide-awake again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears start rolling and I can’t even explain why. I’m not crying all day, but that sad, empty feeling is there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes—maybe not every single day, but a couple of times this week I just broke down. Once was when my mom left after visiting; I closed the door and suddenly felt this wave of loneliness and just sobbed. Another time the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt so useless I ended up crying in the rocker with him in my arms.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… a couple of times, just quick flashes. Like, I’ll be standing at the top of the stairs and picture what if I just fell on purpose—never more than a second or two, and I don’t want to die or anything, but the thought pops in. I haven’t told anyone that.

You've shared how the joy you used to feel has slipped away since your baby arrived: laughter rarely comes, plans feel flat, and a heavy cloud of sadness lingers most of the time. You described feeling overwhelmed, blaming yourself when your little one is fussy, and being bombarded by constant worries about his safety. Nights are especially hard-your mind races, panic surges, and sleep feels impossible. You also admitted that quick, frightening images of self-harm have popped in, though you emphasized you don't want to die.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter or joy, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia) matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame with multiple specific examples, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, uncontrollable, intrusive worries about the baby without real cause, aligning with the highest frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm "most days" and feeling "drowning," indicating intermittent coping difficulties matching "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, prolonged difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing, anxious thoughts—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness "most of the time" with frequent unexplained tears and an ever-present "heavy cloud," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying episodes multiple times this week due to loneliness and feeling useless, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated intrusive self-harm images that occur "a couple of times," matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total ≥14 signals probable major depression; your score of 26 far exceeds this cut-off. You endorse core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: marked <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1, Q2), <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days (Q8), <sym>guilt</sym> (Q3), prominent anxiety/panic (Q4, Q5), and <sym>insomnia</sym> (Q7). Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety evaluation. Together these symptoms suggest moderate-to-severe <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid anxiety and possible <med>postpartum obsessive-compulsive disorder</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (U.S.) or your local crisis line if self-harm thoughts intensify; if imminent risk, go to nearest ED or call emergency services
3. Share these results with your partner or trusted support person so you're not alone with these thoughts
4. Begin basic self-care: accept help with household tasks, aim for brief outdoor walks, and eat small frequent meals to stabilize blood sugar
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when panic sensations start
6. Consider evidence-based treatments: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding-discuss risks/benefits with prescriber
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress after intervention
8. Explore local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or <med>Mom & Baby day programs</med> for peer connection and childcare guidance
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Mood Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery, first child, breastfeeding, partner at home.

Source: Self-reported Edinburgh-style questionnaire.

Symptoms endorsed (frequency ≥ “most days” unless noted):
- Marked anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory pleasure)
- Persistent low mood with daily crying spells
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care
- Unwarranted anxiety and nocturnal panic attacks
- Subjective “drowning” sense of overwhelm
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to rumination
- Fleeting passive self-harm imagery (top-of-stairs fall); denies intent or plan

Pattern: Symptoms cluster consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment evident (sleep, emotional regulation, coping).

Screening significance / risk flags
- Safety: Self-harm ideation present → high-priority safety assessment warranted
- Postpartum depression: meets threshold on core items (mood, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness)
- Postpartum anxiety: prominent generalized and somatic (panic) features
- Psychosocial: social support reduced (lonely after maternal visit), feels “one step behind”

Plan noted for referral
- Immediate safety evaluation and development of crisis plan
- Formal EPDS scoring and clinical interview to confirm severity
- Consideration of perinatal psychiatry and/or mother–infant day program
- Psycho-education and support resources for patient and partner

End note
